metadata.title: TMUA 2022 · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and up to three reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both replace a cosine expression by a quadratic variable, reject algebraic roots outside the cosine range, and count distinct angles with both interval endpoints checked.

The candidate uses a quadratic in absolute cosine instead of cosine squared. Both require range filtering before recovering all permitted positive and negative cosine values and counting their angles.
sharedKnowledge: Solving a quadratic in a cosine expression
Angle counting on a stated interval

matches.rationale: Both recover valid trigonometric levels after algebraic reduction and count their angular solutions over a closed interval. The original factors a quadratic in cosine squared; the candidate takes both signs of a shifted outer square and scales its cosine input.

Both normalise a Cartesian circle equation by completing the two squares and read the squared radius. The candidate directly rehearses the representation needed before the original can impose positivity.

The candidate checks when a circle has a repeated axis intersection and explicitly verifies its positive squared radius. This transfers the original requirement to distinguish a genuine circle from a degenerate equation, with an additional tangency condition.

After the original exposes its squared radius, it needs a strict quadratic sign inequality in a parameter. The candidate specifically practices obtaining and solving such a parameter inequality, including exclusion of equality; its source is a discriminant rather than a radius.

Both recover a function by integrating its derivative and determine an integration constant from a given function value. The original adds one more integration and an integral condition, so the candidate isolates the essential initial-value step.
sharedKnowledge: Using a function value to determine a constant

matches.rationale: Both integrate a known rate and use an initial value to determine the additive constant before imposing or evaluating a further condition. The candidate additionally simplifies its rate first.
sharedKnowledge: Recovering a function from its derivative

matches.rationale: The original must infer constants before advancing a rational recurrence; the candidate supplies the constants and practices the exact remaining skill of substituting a current term into a rational rule while checking its denominator. It does not rehearse the parameter inference.

The original concludes by collecting multiples and sums of logarithms into one logarithm. The candidate practices these same product and power laws when combining exponential factors and taking logs, without the integration step.
sharedKnowledge: Recovering a quantity from a logarithmic equation

matches.rationale: The candidate isolates the original first step: integrate powers and evaluate the whole antiderivative at both bounds. Its bounds are numerical and its powers are less simple; it does not rehearse the logarithmic simplification.
Both calculate an unsigned enclosed area by finding sign changes, splitting the integral and exploiting even symmetry. This rehearses the main distinction between signed integrals and geometric area.

Both remove an absolute value by splitting at its breakpoint before integrating polynomial pieces. The candidate asks for a signed integral, so it tests whether the student follows the requested quantity rather than automatically making every contribution positive.
sharedKnowledge: Splitting an integral at a breakpoint

matches.rationale: Both use symmetry to reduce two polynomial lobes to one integral and then combine unsigned areas. The candidate additionally determines the parameter from a specified total area.

Both relate equal-length blocks of a geometric progression by the power of the common ratio that shifts one block to another, and justify cancelling a nonzero block sum. The candidate uses adjacent blocks, while the original has an intervening block.
sharedKnowledge: Index shifts as powers of the ratio

matches.rationale: The candidate determines a common ratio from a specified term using the correct term exponent, then evaluates a series. This supports the original exponent bookkeeping and ratio recovery, though it uses a convergent progression rather than an increasing integer one.
sharedKnowledge: Checking a ratio against the stated conditions

matches.rationale: Both use the sine-square identity to reduce an algebraic expression to one trig quantity and propagate its attained range to an extremum. The original first eliminates simultaneous function equations and completes a square; the candidate factors a quotient and takes a positive reciprocal.

Both propagate an attained sine range through an outer expression and verify the claimed extreme. The candidate adds exponential and quadratic optimisation; the original first solves pointwise simultaneous function equations. The shared prerequisite is range and attainment, not the entire equation method.

Both translate an input before expanding and compare the resulting polynomial with an intended graph. The candidate adds reflection and stretch, making it a direct check of which coefficients a horizontal or vertical operation changes.

Prerequisite transfer: track how an input scale or translation changes the coordinates of a distinguished graph point. The candidate makes two minimum points coincide; it does not make the whole transformed graphs coincide or repeat the original coefficient-consistency test for a translated cubic.
sharedKnowledge: translate and scale a function input
find transformed point coordinates by equating inner inputs

matches.rationale: The candidate expands a cube and links its coefficients through the same two constants. That is the precise algebra needed to test a translated cubic after its general form is written; the candidate does not require graph transformations.

Both reduce a sum to consecutive integer coefficients and then use an arithmetic-series total. In the original the coefficients arise from logarithm powers; in the candidate they arise from binomial coefficients.

Both first simplify the general summand and then sum the resulting arithmetic progression with the correct index endpoints. The candidate replaces the logarithmic first step by integration and adds a strict threshold check.

The candidate turns a power into a multiplier when taking logarithms. This is the original first step before summing its exponents; the candidate develops it into a straight-line relation and does not practice the finite sum.
sharedKnowledge: Separating a coefficient from a logarithm

matches.rationale: Both reduce a family depending on a real parameter to a quadratic in that parameter and minimise it by its vertex. The candidate obtains the parameter quadratic from a gradient, whereas the original first reads each curve vertex.

Both distinguish the curve variable from its parameter, form a quadratic in that parameter, and locate its minimum. The candidate uses a derivative at a fixed input in place of the original vertex height.
Both minimise a quadratic expression in a real parameter after reducing the original expression. The candidate produces that quadratic by integration; the same completed-square minimum step follows.

Both use a repeated-expression substitution to obtain a quadratic, retain roots in its domain and recover the original quantity. The candidate practises this prerequisite with a positive exponential and logarithms; the original has a nonzero real cube of a product and requires a real cube root.

Both solve an equation by naming a repeated expression and then recover the original quantity from the quadratic roots. The candidate requires nested substitutions and explicit nonnegative filtering, reinforcing the domain check absent from a bare quadratic solution.

The candidate decomposes a circle-inscribed figure into triangles whose equal sides are radii, then computes their areas. This rehearses the original initial use of radii and included angles to obtain an area, while the original alone adds the maximum-altitude argument.
sharedKnowledge: Triangle area from radii and included angle

matches.rationale: The candidate constructs a right triangle from a centre, a radius and a perpendicular to a tangent, then recovers a required length. It practices the specific centre-to-line/right-triangle length calculation needed when the original drops a perpendicular to its chord; it does not teach chord bisection or the area maximum.
sharedKnowledge: Using radii in a geometric auxiliary triangle

matches.rationale: Both parameterise a symmetric inscribed shape by a half-dimension, use the enclosing boundary to eliminate its other dimension, obtain a cubic measure, and use derivative signs to verify the feasible maximum.

Both construct a new polynomial from a transformation of known quadratic roots. The candidate uses square roots and Vieta; the original uses complements of squared trigonometric roots, so both demand reversing the variable transformation correctly.

Both derive a polynomial whose roots are transformed versions of an original quadratic pair. The candidate scales the roots, while the original complements their squares; the common mechanism is constructing coefficients after a root transformation.

Both treat a quartic in even powers as a quadratic in the square, then check what its roots imply for the signed real roots of the quartic. The candidate focuses on positivity and distinctness; those checks validate the original transformed quartic too.
sharedKnowledge: Both treat a quartic in even powers as a quadratic in the square, then check what its roots imply for the signed real roots of the quartic. The candidate focuses on positivity and distinctness; those checks validate the original transformed quartic too.

matches.rationale: Both classify the ambiguous side-side-angle triangle by the altitude and side-length thresholds. The candidate explicitly checks tangency and the degenerate endpoint, the same strict boundaries that determine the original interval for two triangles.

Both must retain acute and obtuse inverse-sine possibilities, enforce a triangle angle sum, and distinguish genuinely noncongruent triangles. The candidate expresses the ambiguity through sine values rather than a variable side length.

Both translate a trigonometric triangle condition into restrictions on variable side lengths and discard degenerate endpoints. The candidate uses the cosine rule and triangle inequality rather than counting the two SSA constructions.

Direct practice of the polynomial root-existence tests used by the original: opposite signs force a root, and an odd-degree leading term supplies opposite tail signs. The candidate assesses whether each condition is sufficient; the original applies these guarantees on disjoint intervals and combines them with a degree bound.
sharedKnowledge: Direct practice of the polynomial root-existence tests used by the original: opposite signs force a root, and an odd-degree leading term supplies opposite tail signs. The candidate assesses whether each condition is sufficient; the original applies these guarantees on disjoint intervals and combines them with a degree bound.

matches.rationale: Counts distinct polynomial roots using signs at ordered inputs and the behaviour of the tails, without solving the polynomial. The candidate derives turning inputs and uses monotonicity to make crossing counts exact; the original samples known factor zeros and uses the polynomial degree as its upper bound.
sharedKnowledge: sign changes on disjoint intervals guarantee distinct roots
justify an upper bound as well as root existence

matches.rationale: Both use strict sign conditions at ordered heights and polynomial tails to guarantee the greatest possible number of distinct roots. The candidate obtains the key heights from stationary points; the original obtains its sample heights where one component polynomial vanishes.
sharedKnowledge: opposite signs guarantee roots in separate intervals
compare the guaranteed count with the polynomial degree
strict height inequalities preserve distinct roots

matches.rationale: The candidate uses the sum and difference of radii at external and internal tangency. Those are precisely the centre-distance boundaries that define the original intersection event before the probability area is calculated.
sharedKnowledge: Internal tangency uses a radius difference
External tangency uses a radius sum

matches.rationale: The candidate reads centres and radii, computes centre distance, and compares it with the sum of radii to measure a boundary gap. This isolates the external-separation test required in the original; it does not practice uniform-area probability or internal containment.
sharedKnowledge: Boundary separation along the line of centres

matches.rationale: Both factor into a linear root and quadratic roots, vary a parameter, and count distinct values after checking repeated roots and overlap between factors. The candidate directly rehearses the exceptional-parameter bookkeeping needed before the original can identify a missing count.
sharedKnowledge: Counting distinct roots at exceptional parameters

matches.rationale: The candidate shows how root counts change at parameter values producing tangency, where a repeated root is only one distinct root. This supports the original boundary-counting step, although the candidate uses turning heights rather than overlap between explicit factors.
